title: Bronchiectasis: Confirm the Structure, Then Control the Cycle
bottomLine: Bronchiectasis is chronic airway dilation with recurrent infection/inflammation and impaired clearance. Confirm the diagnosis with appropriate chest imaging, look for a treatable cause, obtain sputum microbiology when it can change therapy, and build long-term care around airway clearance, vaccination, exacerbation reduction and specialist follow-up when disease is frequent or severe.
recognize: Chronic productive cough, recurrent lower-respiratory infections, daily sputum, hemoptysis and repeated focal radiographic abnormalities are common clues.
Exacerbations are defined clinically by worsening respiratory symptoms rather than a positive sputum culture alone.
differentiate: COPD and asthma can coexist but do not explain permanent bronchial dilation on CT.
Cystic fibrosis, immunodeficiency, aspiration, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, prior infection and ciliary disorders can underlie bronchiectasis and change management.
assessment: Quantify cough/sputum, exacerbation frequency, hemoptysis, dyspnea, weight loss, aspiration/reflux, childhood infections, autoimmune symptoms and prior organisms including Pseudomonas.
Assess oxygenation, clubbing, crackles/wheeze, nutritional status and functional decline.
workup: Use high-resolution chest CT to confirm structural bronchiectasis when clinically indicated and review prior imaging for distribution/progression.
Send sputum for culture during clinically meaningful exacerbation and obtain cause-directed testing for immunodeficiency, CF, ABPA or other etiologies when the phenotype suggests them.
management: Teach individualized airway-clearance techniques, physical activity and vaccination; treat exacerbations with antibiotics selected from severity, prior microbiology and local resistance guidance.

Frequent exacerbations, chronic Pseudomonas infection, significant hemoptysis, declining lung function or uncertain etiology warrants respirology involvement and consideration of long-term specialist-directed therapies.
medicationSafety: Do not prescribe repeated empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics indefinitely without culture history and reassessment.
Long-term macrolide or inhaled-antibiotic strategies require specialist-level indication, interaction/QT/hearing review and antimicrobial-stewardship oversight.
redFlags: New focal imaging concern for obstruction or malignancy
counselling: Teach airway-clearance adherence and an exacerbation action plan, including when sputum change, dyspnea, fever or hemoptysis requires review.
followUp: Track exacerbations, sputum microbiology when indicated, lung function, oxygenation and nutritional/functional status; reassess the underlying cause if the course is atypical.
examTrap: Treating every positive sputum culture as an acute infection or repeatedly prescribing antibiotics without confirming bronchiectasis and reviewing prior microbiology.
oneLinePearl: Bronchiectasis care breaks the infection–inflammation–mucus cycle; CT confirms the structure, the clinical course drives treatment.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society respiratory practice resources

title: Pulmonary Hypertension: Recognize Right-Heart Strain and Find the Cause
bottomLine: Pulmonary hypertension is a hemodynamic syndrome with multiple causes, not a single medication diagnosis. Suspect it with unexplained exertional dyspnea, syncope or right-heart failure, use echocardiography as a probability/risk tool, identify common cardiac/lung/thromboembolic causes, and refer suspected significant disease for specialist confirmation and classification before disease-specific pulmonary vasodilator therapy.
recognize: Progressive exertional dyspnea, fatigue, chest pressure, exertional presyncope/syncope, loud P2, RV heave, JVP elevation and edema are concerning features.
Symptoms may be subtle until right-ventricular reserve is failing.
differentiate: Left-heart disease, chronic lung disease/hypoxia and chronic thromboembolic disease are common causes and require different treatment from pulmonary arterial hypertension.
A high pulmonary pressure estimate on echo does not by itself establish pulmonary arterial hypertension.
assessment: Assess severity, syncope, chest pain, edema, oxygenation, connective-tissue disease, liver disease, HIV/drug exposures, VTE history, sleep-disordered breathing and left-heart/lung disease.
workup: Obtain ECG, chest imaging, echocardiography and pulmonary testing according to presentation; investigate chronic thromboembolic disease and systemic causes when indicated.
Right-heart catheterization is the definitive hemodynamic classification test and belongs in specialist evaluation.
management: Treat hypoxemia and the underlying cardiac/lung/thromboembolic condition when present and refer suspected pulmonary arterial or chronic thromboembolic hypertension to an experienced pulmonary-hypertension program.
Volume overload may require careful diuresis; advanced disease needs specialty-directed therapy and risk assessment.
medicationSafety: Do not start pulmonary arterial hypertension vasodilators solely from an echo estimate before defining the disease group because treatment can be ineffective or harmful in other forms.
Pregnancy with significant pulmonary hypertension is very high risk and requires urgent expert multidisciplinary care.
redFlags: Resting hypoxemia or rapidly worsening dyspnea
Pregnancy with known/suspected significant pulmonary hypertension
counselling: Explain that pulmonary hypertension describes pressure/hemodynamics and that identifying the cause is necessary before choosing disease-specific treatment.
followUp: Specialist follow-up uses symptoms/function, RV status and therapy-specific monitoring; new syncope or congestion should trigger prompt reassessment.
examTrap: Treating an elevated echo-estimated pulmonary pressure as confirmed pulmonary arterial hypertension and starting a vasodilator without classification.
oneLinePearl: Pulmonary hypertension is a syndrome; classify the cause before prescribing the cure.

title: Sarcoidosis: Multisystem Granulomas, Diagnosis of Fit and Exclusion
bottomLine: Sarcoidosis requires a compatible clinical-radiographic syndrome, usually pathologic confirmation when needed, and exclusion of important mimics such as tuberculosis, fungal infection, lymphoma and other granulomatous disease. Not every asymptomatic radiographic case requires corticosteroids; treat threatened organ function or clinically important disease.
recognize: Bilateral hilar/mediastinal adenopathy, pulmonary infiltrates, cough/dyspnea, erythema nodosum, uveitis and hypercalcemia are classic but variable features.
Cardiac and neurologic sarcoidosis may present with conduction disease, ventricular arrhythmia, syncope, focal neurologic deficits or cranial neuropathy and carry higher risk.
differentiate: Granulomas are not specific for sarcoidosis; infection, occupational exposure and malignancy must remain in the differential.
A serum ACE level is neither sufficiently sensitive nor specific to diagnose or exclude sarcoidosis on its own.
assessment: Assess respiratory symptoms, eye symptoms, palpitations/syncope, neurologic symptoms, skin/joint findings, constitutional symptoms, exposure/travel/TB risk and medication history.
workup: Use chest imaging and pulmonary-function assessment; obtain tissue from the safest useful site when confirmation will change management and exclude infectious/malignant mimics.
Use ECG and organ-directed eye, cardiac, neurologic, calcium/renal or liver evaluation when symptoms/risk indicate.
management: Observe selected mild/asymptomatic disease with monitoring; use systemic corticosteroids or steroid-sparing therapy when pulmonary function or another important organ is threatened under specialist guidance.
Cardiac, neurologic or vision-threatening disease requires urgent specialist management.
medicationSafety: Before significant immunosuppression, evaluate infection risk and follow current CTS infection-screening guidance where applicable.
Long-term corticosteroids require metabolic, bone, infection and adrenal-suppression monitoring.
counselling: Explain that some sarcoidosis resolves without treatment while organ-threatening disease requires active therapy and monitoring.
followUp: Track symptoms, pulmonary function/imaging when clinically useful and involved organs; monitor treatment toxicity and relapse.
examTrap: Diagnosing sarcoidosis from bilateral hilar adenopathy plus a high ACE level without excluding TB, fungal disease or lymphoma.
oneLinePearl: Sarcoidosis is a compatible granulomatous syndrome after important mimics are excluded—not a serum ACE diagnosis.

title: Adult Cystic Fibrosis: Multisystem Care in the Modulator Era
bottomLine: Adult cystic fibrosis remains a complex multisystem disease even when CFTR modulators markedly improve health. Care belongs with an accredited multidisciplinary CF program and includes airway/infection surveillance, nutrition, CF-related diabetes/liver/bone disease, fertility/pregnancy, mental health and individualized monitoring of CFTR-modulator therapy.
recognize: Adults may have chronic cough/sputum, recurrent exacerbations, bronchiectasis, sinus disease, pancreatic insufficiency, malnutrition, CFRD, liver disease or male infertility.
CFTR modulators change the expected trajectory but do not eliminate the need for longitudinal CF surveillance.
differentiate: Non-CF bronchiectasis can resemble pulmonary CF but lacks the full diagnostic/genetic/physiologic context.
New respiratory decline in CF may reflect infection, mucus obstruction, ABPA, pneumothorax, hemoptysis or another complication rather than simply 'baseline CF'.
assessment: Review symptoms/exacerbations, airway clearance, microbiology, modulator adherence/tolerance, nutrition/weight, GI symptoms, CFRD, liver/bone disease, fertility/pregnancy and mental health.
workup: Follow the CF program's individualized lung-function, microbiology, imaging and multisystem monitoring schedule.
Use current Canadian CF guidelines for CFTR-modulator initiation/monitoring and complication screening rather than applying generic COPD schedules.
management: Coordinate with the multidisciplinary CF centre; optimize airway clearance, nutrition/pancreatic therapy where indicated, infection management, CFTR-modulator therapy when eligible and complication-specific care.
Acute decline, significant hemoptysis, pneumothorax or severe exacerbation requires prompt CF-team/acute-care involvement.
medicationSafety: CFTR modulators have product-specific hepatic, interaction and reproductive/pregnancy considerations that require current Canadian guidance/monograph review.
Antibiotic doses and regimens in CF can differ from non-CF infections and should follow CF-specific protocols and microbiology.
counselling: Reinforce that feeling much better on modulator therapy does not mean CF monitoring can stop; support reproductive, transition and mental-health planning.
followUp: Maintain multidisciplinary CF clinic follow-up at a frequency matched to disease stage and current Canadian CF standards.
examTrap: Applying ordinary bronchiectasis antibiotic/monitoring rules to an adult with CF without involving CF-specific microbiology, dosing and multidisciplinary care.
oneLinePearl: CFTR modulators changed CF outcomes; they did not turn CF into a single-organ disease.
sourceBasis: Cystic Fibrosis Canada — Canadian Guidelines for Cystic Fibrosis Care
Cystic Fibrosis Canada CFTR Modulator Clinical Consensus Guideline

title: Respiratory Infection in the Immunocompromised Host
bottomLine: Immunocompromised patients can deteriorate with muted fever, WBC response or imaging findings. Define the immune defect, severity and exposures early, broaden the pathogen differential beyond routine CAP, obtain appropriate microbiologic/imaging evidence quickly, and escalate unstable patients before waiting for a classic presentation.
recognize: Neutropenia, transplant, hematologic malignancy, biologic/targeted therapy, high-dose corticosteroids and advanced immune deficiency produce different pathogen risks.
Hypoxemia, tachypnea, confusion or hemodynamic change may be more important than fever.
differentiate: Bacterial pneumonia is only one possibility; Pneumocystis, fungal, viral, mycobacterial and noninfectious drug/immune lung injury can mimic each other.
A normal early chest radiograph does not reliably exclude clinically important infection in some immunocompromised patients.
assessment: Define immune defect, timing of treatment/transplant, prophylaxis, neutrophil count where relevant, exposures/travel, prior organisms, oxygenation and medication toxicities.
workup: Use prompt chest imaging and targeted bacterial/viral/fungal/mycobacterial testing according to risk; obtain cultures before antimicrobials when feasible without delaying treatment in an unstable patient.
Early specialist input and bronchoscopy/BAL may be required when diagnosis remains unclear or disease is severe.
management: Unstable or high-risk patients need hospital-level assessment and empiric therapy matched to immune defect, local epidemiology and prior microbiology, followed by de-escalation when results permit.
Do not manage severe neutropenic or transplant respiratory infection as routine outpatient CAP.
medicationSafety: Renal/hepatic function and major drug interactions matter because antifungals, antivirals and transplant/oncology drugs often interact substantially.
Avoid reflex corticosteroid escalation for presumed inflammatory lung disease until infection risk is appropriately considered.
redFlags: Suspected invasive fungal or Pneumocystis infection
counselling: Teach early contact thresholds because typical fever or sputum changes may be absent during serious infection.
followUp: Close the loop on cultures/PCR/pathology and revise therapy promptly; coordinate with oncology/transplant/immunology/infectious-disease teams.
examTrap: Reassuring a severely immunocompromised patient because they are afebrile and the first chest X-ray is normal.
oneLinePearl: In immunocompromise, absence of classic inflammation is not absence of dangerous infection.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society infection screening before ILD immunosuppression 2026

title: Thoracentesis: Why, Where, and What Can Go Wrong
bottomLine: Thoracentesis is performed to diagnose an unexplained pleural effusion or relieve symptomatic fluid when the expected benefit exceeds procedural risk. Use ultrasound guidance, assess bleeding/respiratory risk, send fluid studies matched to the clinical question, and monitor for pneumothorax, bleeding and re-expansion symptoms.
recognize: New unilateral, atypical, large or clinically unexplained effusions commonly require diagnostic evaluation.
Known transudative causes with a classic response to therapy may not require immediate invasive sampling unless features are atypical.
differentiate: Thoracentesis samples pleural fluid; it does not treat the underlying heart failure, malignancy, infection or thromboembolic disease.
Empyema/complicated parapneumonic effusion may require drainage beyond a one-time diagnostic tap.
assessment: Assess dyspnea/oxygenation, effusion size/location, cause, anticoagulants/antiplatelets, platelet/coagulation issues, positioning tolerance and ultrasound anatomy.
workup: Use bedside or procedural ultrasound to identify a safe pocket.
Order pleural fluid protein/LDH, cell count, pH/glucose, Gram stain/culture, cytology or other studies only as needed by the differential.
management: Use sterile technique and appropriate local procedural protocol; stop and reassess for severe cough, chest pain, dyspnea or instability.
Escalate suspected hemothorax, significant pneumothorax, re-expansion pulmonary edema or ongoing pleural infection.
medicationSafety: Periprocedural antithrombotic management depends on drug, procedure risk, indication and local policy; do not use one universal hold interval.
Avoid unnecessary correction of mildly abnormal coagulation tests when evidence/local procedural policy does not support it.
redFlags: Severe chest pain or re-expansion symptoms
counselling: Explain the diagnostic versus therapeutic purpose and give explicit post-procedure return precautions for dyspnea, chest pain, bleeding or fever.
followUp: Review pleural-fluid results and ensure the underlying cause has an owner; imaging after the procedure is symptom/procedure-context dependent rather than automatically universal.
examTrap: Ordering thoracentesis automatically for every bilateral effusion in a patient with obvious decompensated heart failure before assessing response and atypical features.
oneLinePearl: Thoracentesis answers a pleural question; ultrasound and post-procedure symptoms determine safety.

title: Mechanical Ventilation: Oxygenation, Ventilation, and Lung Protection
bottomLine: Mechanical ventilation supports gas exchange while the cause of respiratory failure is treated. Think in separate problems: oxygenation, ventilation, work of breathing and lung protection. A normal oxygen saturation does not prove adequate ventilation, and escalating pressures without reassessing patient–ventilator mechanics can worsen injury.
recognize: Oxygenation is primarily influenced by FiO2/PEEP and lung recruitment; ventilation depends on effective minute ventilation and dead space.
High airway pressures can reflect decreased compliance, increased resistance, dyssynchrony, secretions, bronchospasm, tube problems or pneumothorax.
differentiate: Peak pressure rises with resistance or compliance problems; plateau pressure more directly reflects static respiratory-system pressure when measured correctly.
Hypoxemia and hypercapnia are different physiologic failures and are not corrected with the same ventilator change.
assessment: Assess the patient first: airway/tube position, chest movement, breath sounds, hemodynamics, oxygenation, mental status/sedation and signs of barotrauma or dyssynchrony.
Review ABG/VBG and ventilator waveforms/pressures in the clinical context.
workup: Use blood gases, chest imaging and cause-directed testing when settings/clinical status change unexpectedly.
If sudden deterioration occurs, rapidly assess tube displacement/obstruction, pneumothorax, equipment failure and acute disease progression.
management: Use lung-protective ventilation for ARDS/at-risk lungs according to critical-care protocols and treat the underlying cause.
Escalate unexplained high pressures, refractory hypoxemia/hypercapnia or hemodynamic collapse to experienced critical-care/respiratory-therapy support immediately.
medicationSafety: Sedation/analgesia should support comfort and synchrony while avoiding unnecessary deep sedation; neuromuscular blockade requires appropriate indication and sedation/monitoring.
Ventilator settings are not medication orders to be adjusted casually outside role/local critical-care protocols.
redFlags: Severe ventilator dyssynchrony or suspected tube obstruction
counselling: For families, explain that the ventilator is supportive therapy while the underlying disease is treated and settings change with physiology.
followUp: Reassess blood gases, pressures, sedation and readiness for liberation as disease improves; prevent ventilator-associated complications through bundle-based care.
examTrap: Responding to a rising PaCO2 by increasing FiO2—or treating a sudden high-pressure alarm by simply raising the alarm limit without assessing the patient.
oneLinePearl: Ventilator reasoning starts with the patient, then asks whether the problem is oxygenation, ventilation, resistance or compliance.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society home/non-invasive ventilation guidance

title: Asthma–COPD Overlap: Preserve Asthma Safety While Treating Fixed Obstruction
bottomLine: Patients can have persistent airflow obstruction with clinically important asthma features. Do not let a COPD label remove inhaled-corticosteroid protection when asthma is genuinely present; confirm obstruction with spirometry, define the dominant traits, address smoking/exposures and exacerbation risk, and individualize inhaled therapy rather than treating 'overlap' as a single disease with one regimen.
recognize: Asthma traits include variable symptoms, atopy/eosinophilic features and greater reversibility/variability; COPD traits include persistent post-bronchodilator obstruction, smoking/exposure history and emphysema/chronic bronchitis phenotype.
Many adults have mixed traits, especially older patients with longstanding asthma or COPD with eosinophilic/variable features.
differentiate: A single bronchodilator response test does not perfectly separate asthma from COPD.
The term overlap describes coexisting traits rather than a separate pathophysiologic diagnosis with unique universal criteria.
assessment: Assess symptom variability, smoking/vaping/occupational exposure, childhood/atopic history, exacerbations, eosinophilic clues, inhaler technique/adherence and comorbidities.
workup: Confirm persistent obstruction with quality spirometry and use additional PFT/imaging only when diagnosis or another disease remains uncertain.
management: When asthma is present, ensure an inhaled-corticosteroid-containing regimen; add bronchodilation according to persistent symptoms/exacerbations and COPD/asthma guidance.
Provide smoking cessation, vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation/activity support when appropriate and written action-plan education.
medicationSafety: Avoid LABA monotherapy in a patient with asthma.
Higher-dose ICS can increase adverse effects including pneumonia risk in COPD-predominant patients; use the lowest effective regimen and reassess indication.
redFlags: Hemoptysis/weight loss or another alternative-diagnosis clue
counselling: Teach that asthma and COPD features can coexist and why controller therapy should not be stopped because day-to-day symptoms improve.
followUp: Track exacerbations, symptoms, technique/adherence and spirometry when clinically useful; reconsider the diagnosis if the course does not fit.
examTrap: Treating a patient with clear asthma features and fixed obstruction using LABA/LAMA alone because the spirometry also looks like COPD.
oneLinePearl: Mixed obstruction still obeys asthma safety: if asthma is truly present, the regimen needs ICS-containing control.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society 2023 COPD Pharmacotherapy Guideline

title: Pulmonary Function Tests: Pattern Before Label
bottomLine: Interpret pulmonary function tests as physiology, not disease labels. Start with test quality, identify obstruction versus restriction or a mixed pattern, use lung volumes to confirm restriction, interpret diffusion capacity in context, and integrate bronchodilator response with the clinical story rather than using one percentage change as a diagnosis.
recognize: Obstruction is identified from the expiratory ratio relative to an appropriate lower limit of normal; restriction requires reduced total lung capacity, not a low FVC alone.
DLCO can fall with emphysema, ILD, pulmonary vascular disease, anemia and other conditions and therefore changes the differential rather than naming one disease.
differentiate: Low FVC with obstruction may represent air trapping rather than true restriction.
Bronchodilator responsiveness supports variable airflow physiology but absence of a significant response does not exclude asthma and presence does not uniquely prove asthma.
assessment: Confirm adequate effort/quality, indication, symptoms, smoking/exposure, prior tests and whether current medications were withheld appropriately for the clinical question.
workup: Use spirometry first for suspected obstructive disease; obtain lung volumes and DLCO when restriction, gas-transfer disease or unexplained symptoms require clarification.
Interpret reference equations without race-based biologic assumptions and follow current CTS recommendations on race/ethnicity in PFT interpretation.
management: Use the physiologic pattern to direct the next diagnostic/management step—obstruction treatment, ILD evaluation, pulmonary vascular workup or further imaging/specialty assessment as indicated.
medicationSafety: Do not escalate inhalers solely from an abnormal PFT without checking symptoms, diagnosis, technique and clinical context.
redFlags: Severe unexplained reduction in gas transfer
Unexpected restrictive physiology or neuromuscular weakness
counselling: Explain that PFTs measure how the lungs work; the final diagnosis still comes from physiology plus clinical context.
followUp: Repeat PFTs when the result will change management or document clinically meaningful progression, not at arbitrary intervals without a question.
examTrap: Calling low FVC 'restrictive lung disease' without measuring total lung capacity—or diagnosing asthma solely from one bronchodilator response.
oneLinePearl: PFTs describe physiology: quality first, pattern second, disease label last.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society Pulmonary Function Testing guidance including 2023 race/ethnicity statement

title: Oxygen Therapy: Treat Hypoxemia, Prescribe the Target
bottomLine: Oxygen is a drug-like therapy with an indication, target and monitoring plan. Treat clinically important hypoxemia and respiratory distress, but do not prescribe chronic oxygen for dyspnea alone without qualifying hypoxemia. In patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, titrate to the ordered target and reassess ventilation rather than reflexively maximizing saturation.
recognize: Acute oxygen is indicated for hypoxemia and selected resuscitation/critical-care situations; chronic home oxygen qualification depends on stable physiologic criteria and local funding/program requirements.
COPD patients with chronic CO2 retention can worsen hypercapnia with excessive uncontrolled oxygen, but needed oxygen should never be withheld from a severely hypoxemic patient.
differentiate: Dyspnea is not synonymous with hypoxemia; opioids, bronchodilation, diuresis, anxiety management or other cause-specific treatment may be more appropriate when saturation is normal.
Pulse oximetry assesses oxygenation, not ventilation; a patient can have acceptable SpO2 with severe hypercapnia.
assessment: Assess SpO2, work of breathing, mental status, perfusion, underlying diagnosis, prior home oxygen and hypercapnia risk.
Confirm whether readings are reliable in poor perfusion, dyshemoglobinemia or other interfering conditions.
workup: Use blood gas assessment when ventilation/acid-base status matters, especially in suspected hypercapnic failure.
For long-term oxygen, use the current Canadian/local program's stable qualifying assessment rather than an acute-exacerbation saturation alone.
management: Titrate oxygen to a defined target appropriate to the clinical context and reassess response.
Treat the underlying cause and arrange respiratory/home-oxygen program follow-up when chronic therapy is initiated or reassessed.
medicationSafety: Avoid routine oxygen in a normoxemic patient solely because chest pain or dyspnea is present.
Oxygen supports combustion; counsel about smoking/open flames and safe equipment use.
redFlags: Need for high oxygen with hemodynamic instability
Suspected pneumothorax or rapidly worsening respiratory failure
counselling: Teach the prescribed flow/device/target, equipment safety and that changing oxygen may not address worsening ventilation or the underlying disease.
followUp: Reassess chronic oxygen need after recovery from an acute illness and according to local home-oxygen criteria; monitor adherence, safety and equipment issues.
examTrap: Giving high-flow oxygen to every dyspneic patient with a normal saturation—or assuming normal SpO2 rules out dangerous hypercapnia.
oneLinePearl: Oxygen treats hypoxemia; saturation is not ventilation, and dyspnea alone is not an oxygen prescription.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society COPD and home ventilation resources
